extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, legal scholars, and law students interested in claim construction and patent doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluation of how patent claim language should be interpreted and constructed by courts and the PTO, including the relative weight of intrinsic and extrinsic evidence, doctrinal rules, and policy considerations. Focuses on doctrinal disputes (Phillips, Markman, Vitronics, etc.) and practical effects on claim drafting and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. §§ 101-103, 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlines the statutory conditions for obtaining a patent (sections 101-103, 112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as the baseline legal framework governing patents; these sections constrain what may properly be claimed and therefore affect claim drafting and claim-scope disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 112 — written description/definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112 governs written description requirements and claim definiteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoked when discussing linguistic certainty and when broad claim language may increase risk of invalidation under § 112; connects to concerns about indefiniteness and ambiguity in claim drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between interpretation and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish 'interpretation' (determining linguistic meaning) from 'construction' (deciding legal effect or scope and applying that meaning to facts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors emphasize the analytic difference and criticize conflation; note that some judicial and scholarly approaches blur the distinction and that advocates may have incentives to conflate meaning and effect to achieve favorable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary and customary meaning as seen by a person of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms should be given the ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases (e.g., Ajinomoto; Multiform Desiccants) describing that PHOSITA reads the patent documents with understanding of field-specific usage; the PHOSITA perspective guides the interpretive baseline and points courts toward intrinsic resources (specification, prosecution history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification (intrinsic record) is highly relevant to claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification contains a written description of the invention and is always highly relevant to claim construction analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Vitronics and Phillips: courts should refer to the specification for linguistic context; authors stress using the specification for ordinary English usage conventions rather than to limit claims to the patentee's inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history can provide relevant linguistic context
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution history, though not physically attached to the claims, may sometimes supply linguistic context for claim meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Liebel‑Flarsheim) show prosecution statements (e.g., deletions or amendments) can inform claim scope; but prosecution history is treated as a separate type of intrinsic evidence and has limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionaries and extrinsic evidence vs. intrinsic record (weighting debate)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate whether claim terms should be interpreted primarily by reference to dictionaries/extrinsic sources or by reference to the intrinsic record (specification and prosecution history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phillips and later cases resolved to give primacy to intrinsic evidence but discussed the role of dictionaries; the text canvasses the split between dictionary-dependent and specification-dependent methodologies and notes the practical implications for public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice and efficiency standard for determining patent scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent scope should be judged by an efficiency/public notice paradigm balancing incentives to innovate against monopoly avoidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Bonito Boats and the economic literature arguing the Patent Clause reflects a balance between encouraging innovation and avoiding monopolies; this policy lens informs normative views about how broadly claims should be read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) during PTO examination
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO examiners use the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' standard when construing claim language in prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Yamamoto and notes PTO's procedural posture calls for a different standard (BRI) than courts use in infringement litigation; this reduces patentee tricks by construing claims broadly during examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee subjective intent is not controlling; emphasize communicated meaning to reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective intent of the applicant or PTO is generally inappropriate; analysis should focus on what is communicated by the language and how a reader would understand it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Markman and Grice: the authors analyze linguistic meaning from the reader's perspective and note that narrow/specific conceptions of patentee intent (as communicated meaning) can be useful but not a license to rely on subjective goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should avoid rewriting claims; role is interpretation not reworking
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial role is limited to interpreting and enforcing agreed text, not rewriting claims to achieve fairness or policy outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases (United States v. Oakland Cannabis Buyers' Coop.; Autogiro; Salvano v. Merrill Lynch) where courts stress their role is interpretation; Farnsworth's contract discussion parallels in showing courts sometimes obscure construction by calling it interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity, vagueness, and generality are distinct and often conflated
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly literature sometimes conflates vagueness, ambiguity, and generality, but they are analytically distinct phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors criticize conflation (Bessen & Meurer, Hovenkamp). They note legal uncertainty (leading to atextual construction) is not the same as linguistic vagueness; some broad terms may be determinate (e.g., 'everything').

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate ambiguity as a patentee strategy — incentives and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees may intentionally use ambiguous or vague claim language to seek broader coverage, but the success of this strategy depends on PTO competence and enforcement incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses literature asserting deliberate ambiguity leads to overbroad patents (Bessen & Meurer; Burk & Lemley). Authors argue the patentee's incentive exists only in a 'Goldilocks' range where the PTO is competent enough to cause fear of rejection but not competent enough to detect deceit; remedy may be improved examiners rather than abolition of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual types matter (linguistic context vs invention-related context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different kinds of context can be relevant to claim meaning, including purely linguistic context and context derived from the subject matter/invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to subsections distinguishing two kinds of 'context' (see Subsection IV.C.3); the general subject matter of the patent can sometimes inform ordinary usage, but that is different from limiting claims to the patentee's inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons and doctrines (avoidance canon, reverse doctrine of equivalents) influence interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrinal tools from statutory and patent law (avoidance canon, reverse doctrine of equivalents) can shape claim construction and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Turrill (avoidance canon), Graver Tank and Roche Palo Alto (reverse doctrine of equivalents) and notes courts' variable application; reverse doctrine of equivalents is rarely affirmed on appeal but remains a doctrinal consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal lens: assess claim meaning as of the filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim meaning is generally assessed at a particular time (e.g., as of the filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Playtex v. Procter & Gamble (claim's meaning assessed as of the filing date) and other authorities emphasizing the relevant temporal perspective for PHOSITA understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial competence, cognitive difficulty, and reversal rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is cognitively demanding; high reversal rates at the Federal Circuit raise questions about judges' ability to resolve highly technical terms without institutional reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites literature (Moore, Lee, Rai) and empirical work on reversal rates; suggests potential procedural responses (e.g., expedited appeals) and highlights selection effects and the difficulty of technical determinations for generalist judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance textual (linguistic) considerations with purpose of the invention (not decisive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may consider the purpose of the invention, but linguistic considerations often carry greater weight; purpose should not be used to rewrite or overly limit the textual meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion of Phillips and its treatment of purpose: majority gave great weight to linguistic considerations while dissent emphasized purpose; commentators (Lemley) criticize outcomes where linguistic readings produce results at odds with invention purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim differentiation and related structural canons affect claim reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines like claim differentiation can constrain how courts read claims relative to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Lemley and Phillips debates: claim differentiation sometimes used to argue against an interpretation that would render certain claims redundant or inconsistent with the claimed embodiments; commentators dispute proper weight and limits.
